title: Designing Google Maps

facts.text: As of March 2021 Google Maps had one billion daily active users and 99% coverage of the world; a simplified design breaks into 3 high-level components: location, map rendering and navigation.
The location service records user location updates, which clients send every few seconds.
Location data is used to detect new and recently closed roads, to improve the map's accuracy over time, and as an input for live traffic data.
The road network is modelled as a graph: intersections are vertices, road sections are edges, and edge weights are the travel time along that section.
Map data can live in a spatial database, which is needed for dynamic data or a huge amount of geographic data and supports spatial queries and geometry manipulation.
For rendering, the world's map is projected into a huge 2D image and broken into tiles. Tiled web maps use Web Mercator, and Google Maps cuts coverage at 85.051129° north and south.
Zoom level 0 shows the whole world in one tile and each level doubles both dimensions, so one tile becomes 4; about 22 zoom levels are sufficient for most practical purposes.
Clients request tiles by URL such as .../Z/X/Y.png. On a pan most displayed tiles stay relevant and only new ones are fetched, which beats fetching one image for the whole viewport.
Tiles are static and rarely change, so a CDN backed by cloud storage like S3 serves them, and users load the tiles they need from a nearby CDN.
To support zooming and panning, pre-calculate the map blocks at different zoom levels and load the images when needed; pre-computing individual tiles is easy to parallelize.
The navigation service finds a reasonably fast route from point A to point B, calling a Geocoding Service to resolve an address to a latitude/longitude pair and a Route Planner Service.
Geocoding matches an address to a street segment whose address range includes the house number and interpolates the position within that range.

The Route Planner calculates the top-K shortest paths between A and B, estimates the time of each path from current traffic and historical data, then ranks the paths by predicted time and user filtering.

Plain Dijkstra's algorithm is impractical on networks with tens of millions of vertices. A* with a straight-line-distance heuristic helps, but is generally outperformed by algorithms that pre-process the graph.

Contraction hierarchies precompute shortcuts, spending seconds to hours once because roads change rarely, then answer queries in microseconds with a bidirectional search that only climbs toward more important vertices.

When live traffic changes edge weights more often than the road topology, a customization phase re-applies the stored contractions with new weights and can honor preferences such as avoiding ferries or highways.

notes: thin: the sources give no functional requirements, storage estimates, API, ETA model or live-traffic ingestion pipeline, and no failure handling. The toll example (bcd4187fdc2f) reads 'the user doesn't want to avoid tolls', probably a typo, so the user-filtering fact stays general; the customization sentence supports avoiding road types.

definition.text: A world map projected into one huge 2D image and cut into small image blocks that the client joins seamlessly, each requested separately.

facts.text: The world's map is projected into a huge 2D image and broken into small blocks called tiles, which the client joins seamlessly into the visible map.
When the user pans, most tiles stay relevant and only new ones are fetched. Tiles can be pre-computed in parallel, and serving rendered images is cheaper than rendering in the browser.

Common conventions: zoom level 0 shows the whole world in one tile, each zoom level doubles both dimensions so one tile becomes 4, about 22 levels suffice, and Web Mercator is used with latitude limits near 85 degrees.
The OpenStreetMap XYZ convention serves tiles at URLs like .../Z/X/Y.png, with Z the zoom level and X and Y identifying the tile. Tile Map Service numbers Y northwards, OpenStreetMap southwards.
Tiles are static and rarely change, so a CDN backed by cloud storage such as S3 serves them efficiently, and users load the tiles they need from a nearby CDN.

To support zooming and panning, the map blocks are pre-calculated at different zoom levels and the images are loaded when needed. A single file holding all tiles, as PMTiles does, is an alternative with good performance.
Most tiles are raster images such as PNG or JPEG. Vector tiles are rendered by the client, which can style them and keep text readable when rotating; Google and Apple have moved to vector tiles.
A web mapping framework such as the Google Maps API, OpenLayers or Leaflet retrieves, displays and caches the tiles and handles user navigation.

definition.text: An algorithm that finds the shortest paths from a source node to every other node in a weighted graph, such as a road network.

facts.text: It starts with distance zero at the source and infinity elsewhere, then repeatedly picks the unvisited vertex with the lowest distance and updates each unvisited neighbor's distance if the route through that vertex is shorter.
It computes shortest paths from the source to every other node, and can stop as soon as the shortest path to one chosen destination is known.

A min-priority queue selects the closest vertex. A binary heap gives O((V+E) log V); Fibonacci heaps have better theoretical bounds but often perform worse in real applications because of large constant factors.

Sparse networks such as road maps suit it. Modern routing systems pair it with preprocessing such as A*, landmark heuristics or contraction hierarchies; contraction hierarchies can be up to seven orders of magnitude faster.
It gives incorrect results when edges have negative weights, because its greedy strategy finalizes a vertex's distance before a cheaper path through a negative edge is seen.

Starting with a queue holding only the source and inserting vertices as they are discovered gives uniform-cost search, which can find the closest of a set of targets even on graphs too large to hold in memory.

Bidirectional Dijkstra searches forward from the source and backward from the target on the reversed graph, stopping when the two queues' minimum priorities sum to at least the best path found; it explores far fewer vertices on road-like graphs.
Shortest-path algorithms are used in network routing protocols, most notably IS-IS and OSPF.

definition.text: A graph search algorithm that finds the cheapest path from a start node to a goal node by extending the path with the lowest cost so far plus an estimate of the cost still to go.

facts.text: A* is an informed, best-first search on a weighted graph. It keeps a tree of paths from the start node and extends them one edge at a time until the goal is reached.
It extends the path that minimizes f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the cost from the start to n and h(n) is a problem-specific heuristic estimating the cheapest remaining path to the goal.
Implementations keep the frontier in a priority queue ordered by f, stop when the node removed is the goal, and store each node's predecessor to recover the path.
On a road map the heuristic can be the straight-line distance to the goal, the physically smallest possible distance; on a grid map, taxicab or Chebyshev distance fits better.
A* returns an optimal path when the heuristic is admissible. With a consistent heuristic it never processes a node more than once and equals Dijkstra's algorithm run with a reduced edge cost.
Dijkstra's algorithm is the special case where h(x) = 0 for all nodes. A* differs from greedy best-first search because it also counts the distance already travelled.

Search effort depends on the heuristic: a close estimate cuts node expansions and a poor one causes many. Relaxing admissibility trades optimality for speed, with ε-admissible variants guaranteed within (1 + ε) of optimal.

A* keeps all generated nodes in memory, its biggest practical drawback. In travel-routing systems it is generally outperformed by algorithms that pre-process the graph, though it is still the best solution in many cases.

definition.text: A speed-up technique for shortest-path queries that precomputes shortcuts in a road graph so a query can skip unimportant vertices.

facts.text: A road network is a graph with intersections as vertices and road sections as edges weighted by travel time. Dijkstra's algorithm is impractical on it because road networks have tens of millions of vertices.
The method has a preprocessing phase and a query phase. Road networks change rarely, so seconds to hours can be spent once, and queries are then answered in microseconds.

Road networks are highly hierarchical: highway junctions rank above a junction into a dead end. A shortcut joins two non-adjacent vertices with the weight of their shortest path, so queries skip the full path between important junctions.
Preprocessing contracts vertices one by one: it removes a vertex and adds a shortcut between two neighbors only if their shortest path goes through it, which a witness search checks.

The contraction order should add few shortcuts, but optimal ordering is NP-complete, so heuristics are used. Bottom-up heuristics are cheaper and greedy; top-down heuristics give better results but need more preprocessing time.
A query runs a bidirectional search from the start and target over the graph plus shortcuts. Both searches only follow edges to more important vertices, which keeps the search space small.
A query yields the travel time or distance, not the route. Shortcuts must be unpacked into road edges, and storing each shortcut's middle vertex makes the recursive unpacking linear-time.

If edge weights change more often than the road topology, a customization phase between preprocessing and query can switch between distance and time, include current traffic, or honor user preferences such as avoiding ferries or highways.

definition.text: A variant of the Mercator map projection that applies spherical formulas to WGS 84 coordinates and is the standard for web mapping.

facts.text: Virtually all major online map providers use it, including Google Maps, Mapbox, Bing Maps and OpenStreetMap; its identifier is EPSG:3857.
It uses spherical formulas at all scales on WGS 84 coordinates, which makes it slightly non-conformal, but the spherical form needs only a fraction of the computing resources of the ellipsoidal one.
World coordinates are scaled so the upper left corner is (0, 0) and the lower right is (2^zoom - 1, 2^zoom - 1) before pixel positions are computed at a zoom level.
Mercator projects the poles at infinity, so Web Mercator cannot show them; Google Maps cuts off coverage at 85.051129° north and south, the latitude at which the full map becomes a square.

definition.text: Turning a text description of a location, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates, usually a latitude and longitude pair.

facts.text: Reverse geocoding converts coordinates back to a description such as a place name or address. Geocoding relies on representations of address points, the street network, and postal and administrative boundaries.

A geocoder combines an input dataset of descriptive text, a reference dataset of feature locations in a spatial reference system, and software that matches each input to a reference feature and attaches its location.

A direct match maps an input to one whole reference feature, such as a country or ZIP code, much like a table join but with handling for approximate matches such as different capitalization or slight misspellings.

Address interpolation uses street segments tagged with address ranges. The geocoder parses the address, matches a segment whose number range includes it, and estimates the position along that segment.
Positional accuracy varies, from building centroids and interpolated street positions to postal code and administrative-division centroids.

Mismatches arise from misspelled or incomplete input and outdated reference data. Geocoders handle abbreviations such as E for East, and cleaning the input, called address scrubbing, improves accuracy.
Ambiguity such as the same street name in two towns is resolved by asking for the city and region.
On the web, geocoding powers routing and local search. A geohash is a grid-style geocode that encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string.
